beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. You know LLMs, they generate text. But there's a different kind of model showing up, built to make one fast decision your code can actually use. It's called a System One model. Let's see what it is, and when you'd reach for it instead of a chatbot.

props.command: What's a “System One model” — and how is it different from an LLM I'd chat with?
output: made for software to act on

beats.narration_text: Definition first. A System One model reads a state, some text, and returns a typed answer with a probability. Not a paragraph you have to parse, an actual value: a category, a score, or a yes-or-no, plus how confident it is. TypeSafe's model, Jev, is the first of these. Think fast, structured judgment, not conversation.

show.event: the state chip feeds the model
the model outputs a typed answer + confidence (accent)

card.title: Not Text — a Decision.
card.subtitle: the definition, first
card.caption: it reads a state and returns a typed answer with a probability — not a paragraph to parse
card.footer: STATE IN · TYPED DECISION + PROBABILITY OUT

beats.narration_text: Here's the split. An LLM generates free-form text, and your code has to read it back out and hope the format holds. A System One model returns a typed decision directly, already shaped for software. Same natural-language input, completely different output. One writes; the other decides.

show.event: the two columns build in parallel
the System One column resolves to a typed decision (accent)

card.title: LLM vs System One.
card.subtitle: same input, different output
card.caption: one writes; the other decides
card.footer: GENERATES TEXT  vs  RETURNS A TYPED DECISION

beats.narration_text: You define the answer space up front, with three primitives. Choice: pick one option, like which team gets this ticket. Score: a number on a scale, like how frustrated a customer is. And Noul: a true-or-false, like, is this a refund request? Every answer comes back typed, and with a probability.

show.event: the three primitive cards snap in

card.title: Three Primitives.
card.subtitle: you define the answer space

items.quote: a number on a scale — e.g. 1.4

card.caption: every answer comes back typed — and with a probability
card.footer: CHOICE · SCORE · NOUL — ALL ILLUSTRATIVE VALUES

beats.narration_text: The interesting part is that probability. System One models are trained to be calibrated, their confidence is tuned against real outcomes. But read the fine print: calibration holds across groups of predictions, not any single answer. So a ninety-five percent doesn't mean this one is right, it means you can set a threshold, and act or escalate.

card.title: Confidence You Can Use.
card.subtitle: calibrated, with fine print

items.quote: not a guarantee for one answer
set a threshold: act or escalate

card.caption: a 95% means the group is right ~95% of the time — not that this one is

beats.narration_text: Watch it work. A refund request comes in. You build a state, the customer's message, their transactions, the policy. You ask three questions at once: was a refund requested, does the evidence show a duplicate charge, does the policy allow it. Each comes back typed, with confidence. Then plain code combines them, and routes the case, act, or send to a human.

show.event: the state tiles feed the model
the answer resolves: code routes act or escalate (accent)

card.title: One Decision, In a Workflow.
card.subtitle: a refund request
card.answer: refund asked? · duplicate? · policy ok? → code routes: act, or escalate
card.caption: typed answers combine with plain code into a predictable workflow

beats.narration_text: So when do you reach for it? When you need a fast, structured decision code can branch on. Not when you need writing, it doesn't produce replies, code, or explanations, that's still an LLM's job. And when its confidence is low, you escalate, to a person, or to a slower reasoning model. Right tool, right job.

show.event: the two columns build: LLM job vs System One job

card.title: When to Reach For It.
card.subtitle: decide vs write
card.caption: it doesn't write replies, code, or explanations — that's still an LLM's job
card.footer: DECIDE → SYSTEM ONE · WRITE / REASON → LLM

beats.narration_text: So, a System One model reads a state and returns a typed, calibrated decision your software can act on. Fast judgment, not conversation. Use it to decide, use an LLM to write, and let the confidence tell you when to hand off.

props.artifactHeading: What it is, when to use it
artifactLines: A System One model reads a state (text) and returns a TYPED answer + a calibrated probability — not generated text.
Define the answer space with primitives: Choice (pick one), Score (a number), Noul (true/false).
Calibration holds across groups, not any single answer — use confidence to set act-vs-escalate thresholds.
Reach for it for fast decisions code can branch on; use an LLM to write or reason. Jev is TypeSafe's first.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Find one place in your work where you're using a chatbot just to get a yes-or-no or a category, and then parsing its text. Write down the typed question you actually want answered, and the confidence threshold where you'd stop and check yourself. That's a System One shaped problem.
